title: Who’s in, Who’s Out? Analyzing the USMNT’s Depth Chart After November International Window
subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Sophia Vesely, Amanda Langell6:15 PM ESTThe USMNT has never had such depth. / Robin Alam/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesManager Mauricio Pochettino may have walked through the exit door after the November international break, but before he did, he left the U.S. men’s national team quite the parting gift: depth.

The Argentine boss left no stone unturned in his search for the nation’s brightest talents. In two years at the helm, Pochettino gave 31 Americans their senior debuts, and over 75 players total earned at least one cap.

The previous window—the extended September-October camp—was one of Pochettino’s most experimental, seeing him bring in 12 debutants, including eight teenagers. Pochettino’s trust was repaid tenfold, as the USMNT cruised to four straight wins with seven of its 12 goals coming from those American kids, one of whom even became the youngest goalscorer in USMNT history.

Pochettino took things a step further in November, cap-tying eight of those burgeoning talents, including 17-year-old prodigy Cavan Sullivan, meaning they will only be able to represent the Stars and Stripes on the international stage moving forward.

The 2030 World Cup might still be four years away, but the new manager will nonetheless be eager to zero in on his best squad, one capable of finally making a deep run on the biggest stage in soccer. Thanks to Pochettino, there will be plenty of talent at the successor’s disposal, a healthy mix of  established veterans and exciting, unproven teenagers—but where do they all stack up?

Sports Illustrated’s deep dive into the USMNT’s depth breaks down the Stars and Stripes’ best players at every position. The guide only includes players that have been rostered in the last 12 months, dating back to November 2025. Former captain Tim Ream is excluded following his retirement.

The rankings are not only based on current success, but also level of potential, especially when it comes to the young players, such as Brooklyn Raines, Neil Pierre and Mathis Albert, all of whom have a high ceiling.

Diego Kochen played every minute of the November window. / Omar Vega/USSF/Getty ImagesDiego Kochen (Lyngby)Brian Schwake (Nashville SC)Chris Brady (Chicago Fire)Matt Freese (NYCFC)Patrick Schulte (Columbus Crew)Roman Celentano (FC Cincinnati)Jonathan Klinsmann (Cesena)Matt Turner (New England Revolution)At the 2026 World Cup, it was Matt Freese between the posts for the USMNT. But a disastrous outing against Belgium was the final straw for the inconsistent, mistake-prone goalkeeper. He might’ve still logged 45 minutes against Peru in September, but he soon watched three other names jump above his on the depth chart. Pochettino has been Freese’s biggest champion, but with him no longer in the picture, Freese may count himself lucky to get a call up at all.

Chris Brady, Diego Kochen, and Brian Schwake shared the rest of the minutes in the September-October window, suggesting that even Pochettino knew that it was time for the team to move past Freese as the automatic starter. Twenty-year-old Kochen played the full 90 minutes and kept a clean sheet in the team’s 3–0 win against bitter rival Mexico, meanwhile becoming the youngest goalkeeper to ever start a game for the USMNT. Nevertheless, it was Schwake who left the fall window having made two starts and a better impression. His brick wall persona was soon emphasized when he tied MLS’s single season shutout record (16) for Nashville SC by the end of the season.

Both Schwake and Kochen earned second consecutive call ups for November, alongside Freese; however, this time, it was Kochen who really made his mark. He played all 180 minutes of the two-legged Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals tie against Haiti and earned another two shutouts. He has yet to concede a goal on the senior international stage.
Although the Barcelona academy graduate has yet to really be put to the test, he has all the makings of a superstar, confident in his distribution and in coming off his line to make big saves.
Schwake will no doubt keep pressure on Kochen and may even turn the new manager’s head should he lead Nashville to the 2026 MLS Cup as expected next month.

Antonee Robinson is a stalwart on the left flank. / Michael Miller/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesAlex Freeman (Villarreal)Antonee Robinson (Fulham)Joe Scally (Borussia Mönchengladbach)Peyton Miller (New England Revolution)Francis Westfield (Philadelphia Union)Bryan Reynolds (Rennes)Reed Baker-Whiting (Nashville SC)John Tollkin (Holstein Kiel)Antonee Robinson and Alex Freeman have come to own the flanks.

While veteran Robinson has long commanded the left side, Freeman proved his worth at the World Cup. There were initial doubts over whether he could hang with the best, but the 22-year-old quickly silenced all doubters this summer. He has only improved this fall, not only maintaining his consistency on the international stage in both windows, but also making more of a name for himself in La Liga. Freeman stunned both Real Madrid and Barcelona with his athleticism, speed and creativity down the flank, playing 90 minutes in each affair while forcing the European giants to fight for narrow wins.

Joe Scally will feel grateful Pochettino left the federation. No matter how much magic the 23-year-old conjures for club side Borussia Mönchengladbach, it’s never enough for the Argentine. After a limited role off the bench at the World Cup this summer, Scally was excluded from both the September-October and the November windows, despite enjoying the most prolific season of his career (three goals and three assists thus far).

As Scally climbs his way back up the depth chart, he will certainly have 19-year-old Peyton Miller and 21-year-old Frankie Westfield at his heels, both of whom made their debuts last month. Miller and Westfield were key figures in MLS this season for New England Revolution and Philadelphia Union respectively.

Chris Richards is irreplaceable. / Jeff Dean/USSF/Getty ImagesChris Richards (Crystal Palace)Auston Trusty (Celtic)Mark McKenzie (Toulouse)George Campbell (West Bromwich Albion)Neil Pierre (Philadelphia Union)Miles Robinson (FC Cincinnati)Five of these center backs are essentially fighting for one spot. Chris Richards is irreplaceable in the USMNT’s starting XI as the team’s defensive leader, both on and off the pitch.

There is a Ream-shaped hole alongside Richards, though. Throughout the fall, Auston Trusty has steadily proved himself most trustworthy—no pun intended—to succeed the veteran captain, who announced his international retirement in October. Trusty harbors similar poise and leadership capabilities to Richards, with an equal aerial dominance. The two worked off each other brilliantly against Mexico and Haiti, the latter in which Trusty actually scored.

Keep an eye out for Neil Pierre, though. The 18-year-old, who made his debut in September, is expected to be the long-term replacement for Ream. He earned another call up in November, featuring for 45 minutes in the second leg against Haiti. The towering center back is brilliant in the air and has a knack for goal, but must hone his skills in order to one day beat out Trusty, Mark McKenzie or George Campbell.
